lessons.body:
# `this` is bound at the call site

Unlike closures (lexical), `this` is **dynamic**: it's set by *how the function is called*, not where it's defined. To determine `this`, find the call site and apply the rules in precedence order.

## The four rules

**1. Default binding.** A bare call — `foo()` — with no other rule applying. In strict mode `this` is `undefined`; in sloppy mode it's the global object. ES modules are always strict, so expect `undefined`.

**2. Implicit binding.** Called as a method: `obj.foo()` sets `this` to `obj` — whatever is left of the dot *at the call site*.

**3. Explicit binding.** `foo.call(obj, ...)`, `foo.apply(obj, [...])`, or a bound function from `foo.bind(obj)` — `this` is the object you passed.

**4. `new` binding.** `new Foo()` creates a fresh object, sets it as `this`, and returns it (unless the constructor returns its own object).

## Precedence

`new` beats explicit, which beats implicit, which beats default:

```js
function show() { return this.name; }

show.call({ name: 'explicit' });              // explicit beats default
const bound = show.bind({ name: 'bound' });
bound.call({ name: 'other' });                // 'bound' — bind is permanent
```

A bound function's `this` cannot be overridden — not by `call`, not by `apply`, not by another `bind`. (`new` outranks explicit binding for `this`, while keeping any preset arguments — interview trivia worth knowing.)

## The bug this system produces

Method extraction drops implicit binding:

```js
const user = {
  name: 'Ada',
  greet() { return `hi ${this.name}`; },
};
const g = user.greet;
g(); // strict: TypeError — `this` is undefined
```

`g()` is a default-binding call; nothing is left of the dot anymore. This single mechanic — detaching a method from its object — causes more production `this` bugs than the other three rules combined.

## Nested functions don't inherit this

```js
const obj = {
  name: 'obj',
  outer() {
    function inner() { return this.name; } // `this` is NOT obj
    return inner(); // default binding — undefined in strict mode
  },
};
```

Every `function` gets its own `this` from its own call site. (Arrow functions are the exception — two lessons from now.)
lessons.comparisonNote: Java's `this` is always the enclosing instance — lexical, predictable, boring in the best way. JavaScript's `this` is re-decided at every call site. The Java instinct to transfer: read `this` as "whatever was left of the dot when this function was invoked." When nothing was left of the dot, that's your bug.
keyPoints: `this` is bound dynamically at the call site — find the call, then apply the rules.
Precedence: `new` > explicit (`call`/`apply`/`bind`) > implicit (`obj.m()`) > default.
Extracting a method (`const g = obj.m; g()`) drops implicit binding — the most common production bug.
Nested `function`s get their own `this`; they never inherit the outer one.
In strict mode (all modules, all classes) default binding is `undefined`, not the global object.
lessons.title: The Four Binding Rules & Precedence

lessons.body:
# Explicit binding, three flavors

```js
function introduce(greeting, punctuation) {
  return `${greeting}, I'm ${this.name}${punctuation}`;
}
const ada = { name: 'Ada' };

introduce.call(ada, 'Hello', '!');     // 'Hello, I'm Ada!'
introduce.apply(ada, ['Hello', '!']);  // same — args as an array
const bound = introduce.bind(ada, 'Hi');
bound('?');                            // "Hi, I'm Ada?"
```

- **`call(thisArg, ...args)`** — invokes immediately, arguments listed out.
- **`apply(thisArg, [args])`** — invokes immediately, arguments as an array. Spread syntax (`f(...args)`) has replaced most `apply` call sites, but it survives wherever the receiver must be explicit.
- **`bind(thisArg, ...presetArgs)`** — does *not* invoke. Returns a new function with `this` permanently fixed and leading arguments pre-filled.

## bind is permanent and partial

A bound function's `this` cannot be overridden — not by `call`, not by `apply`, not by another `bind`. But `bind` also presets arguments, which makes it a partial-application tool independent of `this`:

```js
function log(level, msg) { console.log(`[${level}] ${msg}`); }
const warn = log.bind(null, 'WARN'); // `this` irrelevant here
warn('disk full'); // '[WARN] disk full'
```

## Where explicit binding shows up

- **Borrowing array methods** for array-likes: `Array.prototype.map.call(document.querySelectorAll('li'), fn)` — works because the builtin only needs a `length` and indexed access, not a real array.
- **Fixing callbacks:** `setTimeout(obj.method.bind(obj), 100)` keeps the receiver across the async boundary.
- **Library code** that invokes user callbacks with a chosen receiver (event systems setting `this` to the emitter, for example).

## Interview trivia: bind + new

`new (fn.bind(thisArg, ...preset))()` ignores `thisArg` (the fresh object wins — `new` outranks explicit binding) but keeps the preset arguments. Rarely used, frequently asked.
lessons.comparisonNote: Java has no equivalent because Java method receivers are fixed — you can't invoke `obj.method()` "as if" it belonged to someone else. The closest mental model is a Java method reference with a captured receiver (`this::handleClick`): `bind` produces a function value with its receiver baked in. The JS superpower Java lacks is rebinding that receiver explicitly at the call site with `call`.
keyPoints: `call`/`apply` invoke immediately with an explicit receiver; `bind` returns a new permanently-bound function.
`apply`'s array form is largely replaced by spread; `call` and `bind` remain daily tools.
A bound `this` can't be overridden by later `call`/`apply`/`bind`.
`bind` doubles as partial application — preset leading arguments with any receiver.
Method borrowing works because builtins like `map` only need the right *shape*, not a real array.
lessons.title: call, apply & bind

lessons.comparisonNote: Java lambdas also capture `this` lexically — the enclosing instance — so arrows are the one corner of JavaScript where `this` behaves the way a Java developer expects. The difference is syntactic discipline: Java *separates* lambdas from methods, so you can't accidentally write a "method lambda." JS arrows look like shorthand functions, which is exactly why they get misused as object methods and constructors.
keyPoints: Arrow functions have no own `this` — they inherit it lexically from the enclosing scope.
Arrows are the default for callbacks inside methods; they replaced the `const self = this` pattern.
Never use arrows for object methods needing dynamic `this`, constructors, or anything needing `arguments`.
Class-field arrows bind per instance: convenient for handlers, with memory/subclassing tradeoffs.
Arrows can't be constructed (`new` throws) and have no `prototype`.
lessons.title: Arrow Functions & Lexical this

lessons.comparisonNote: Java frameworks detach callbacks constantly (Spring handlers, Android listeners), but a Java method reference like `this::onClick` carries its instance with it — it can't lose its receiver. In JavaScript the function and the receiver are separable values, so *every* callback boundary is a potential lost-`this`. Treat each one like a method reference that forgot its instance, and bind or wrap accordingly.
keyPoints: The receiver doesn't travel with the function: `setTimeout(obj.m, t)` and destructuring both drop it.
Fix lost receivers with an arrow wrapper (preserves the call site) or `bind` (bakes in the receiver).
DOM handlers set `this` to the element only for non-arrow functions.
Modules and classes are always strict: detached calls fail fast with `this === undefined`.
Debug with the five-step drill: call site → `new` → explicit → left-of-dot → default.
